items.q: What is the primary physiological mechanism responsible for benign early decelerations observed on an intrapartum cardiotocography trace?
o: Increased intracranial pressure during uterine contractions stimulating the vagus nerve
Uteroplacental insufficiency with anaerobic myocardial metabolism
Transient occlusion of the umbilical vein baroreceptors
Maternal systemic hypotension following epidural analgesia
items.exp: Early decelerations are physiological and benign, caused by mechanical compression of the fetal head against the maternal pelvis or cervix during contractions. Head compression alters cerebral blood flow and raises intracranial pressure, stimulating central vagal baroreceptors and slowing the fetal heart rate in exact synchrony with the contraction.
r: Correct. Head compression increases intracranial pressure, stimulating vagal slowing that mirrors contractions.
Incorrect. Uteroplacental insufficiency causes late decelerations, which are pathological.
Incorrect. Umbilical cord occlusion causes abrupt variable decelerations.
Incorrect. Maternal epidural hypotension causes prolonged decelerations or bradycardia.
items.kp: Early decelerations mirror contractions exactly and are caused by benign fetal head compression stimulating the vagus nerve.

items.q: A cardiotocography trace during active labor demonstrates repetitive, symmetrical, gradual decelerations whose onset occurs after the peak of each contraction, with the nadir occurring after the contraction peak and recovery delayed until after the contraction ends. What is this deceleration pattern?
items.exp: Late decelerations are defined by their delayed timing: onset occurs at or after the peak of uterine contraction, the nadir occurs after the contraction peak, and recovery occurs only after the contraction has fully relaxed. They reflect uteroplacental hypoperfusion, fetal arterial hypoxemia, and chemoreceptor-mediated vagal deceleration.
r: Correct. Symmetrical decelerations lagging behind contractions are late decelerations, indicating uteroplacental insufficiency.
Incorrect. Early decelerations mirror contractions simultaneously without lag.
Incorrect. Variable decelerations are abrupt and variable in timing.
Incorrect. Sinusoidal pattern is a continuous undulating sine wave.
items.kp: Late decelerations lag behind uterine contractions and reflect uteroplacental hypoperfusion and fetal hypoxia.

items.q: What is the normal reference range for baseline fetal heart rate variability on an intrapartum cardiotocography trace?
items.exp: Normal baseline fetal heart rate variability (beat-to-beat variability) is defined as fluctuations in the baseline FHR of 5 to 25 beats per minute. Normal variability reflects a healthy, well-oxygenated fetal autonomic nervous system and intact brainstem pacemaking coordination.
r: Correct. Normal baseline variability is 5 to 25 bpm, indicating intact fetal central oxygenation.
Incorrect. < 5 bpm represents reduced/minimal variability, non-reassuring if prolonged.
Incorrect. > 25 bpm represents saltatory (marked) variability, seen in acute hypoxia.
Incorrect. 30 to 45 bpm represents severe marked instability.
items.kp: Normal baseline fetal heart rate variability is 5 to 25 beats per minute.

items.q: An intrapartum cardiotocography trace reveals a regular, smooth, undulating sine wave-like pattern with a frequency of 3 to 5 cycles per minute and an amplitude of 10 bpm, persisting for over 30 minutes with completely absent normal variability and no accelerations. What does this pathognomonic pattern indicate?
o: Severe fetal anemia or profound fetal acidemia
items.exp: A true sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern is a smooth, undulating sine wave lasting > 20-30 minutes, with regular oscillation frequency of 3-5 cycles/min and amplitude of 5-15 bpm, with absent baseline variability. It is pathognomonic for severe fetal anemia (Rh isoimmunization, fetomaternal hemorrhage, ruptured vasa previa) or severe pre-terminal fetal asphyxia.
r: Correct. A true sinusoidal pattern indicates severe fetal anemia or severe asphyxia, demanding urgent intervention.
Incorrect. Fetal sleep produces reduced variability, but not an undulating sine-wave oscillation.
Incorrect. Umbilical cord compression causes abrupt variable decelerations.
Incorrect. Maternal hyperventilation does not produce a sinusoidal trace.
items.kp: A sinusoidal CTG pattern is pathognomonic for severe fetal anemia or profound asphyxia, requiring urgent delivery.

items.q: What is the initial non-operative resuscitation maneuver for managing repetitive variable decelerations on CTG caused by umbilical cord compression?
o: Repositioning the mother into the left lateral position
Immediate emergency cesarean delivery without repositioning
Administration of high-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate
items.exp: Variable decelerations are caused by umbilical cord compression between the fetal body and uterine wall. The immediate first-line intrauterine resuscitation maneuver is maternal repositioning into the left or right lateral decubitus position (or knee-chest position). This alters the intrauterine gravitational vector, relieving mechanical cord compression in over 50% of cases.
r: Correct. Maternal lateral repositioning is the first-line intervention to relieve mechanical cord compression.
Incorrect. Oxytocin increases uterine contractions, worsening cord compression and fetal hypoxia.
Incorrect. Immediate cesarean is premature before attempting rapid conservative positional correction.
Incorrect. Magnesium sulfate is for neuroprotection in preterm labor, not acute variable decelerations.
items.kp: Maternal repositioning to the lateral decubitus position is the first-line measure to relieve variable decelerations.

items.q: A fetal scalp blood sample is obtained from a fetus with a pathological intrapartum CTG trace showing repetitive late decelerations. What fetal scalp pH value indicates severe fetal acidosis warranting immediate delivery?
items.exp: Fetal scalp blood sampling interpretation guidelines establish: scalp pH >= 7.25 is normal and reassuring (labor may continue); pH 7.21 to 7.24 is borderline (repeat sampling in 30 minutes); and pH < 7.20 indicates significant fetal acidosis, mandating immediate expedited operative delivery.
r: Correct. Fetal scalp pH < 7.20 indicates significant acidosis requiring immediate expedited delivery.
Incorrect. pH 7.25 to 7.35 is normal and labor may continue safely.
Incorrect. pH > 7.30 is completely normal.
Incorrect. pH 7.21 to 7.24 is borderline, managed by repeat sampling in 30 minutes.
items.kp: A fetal scalp blood pH < 7.20 confirms significant fetal acidosis and mandates immediate delivery.

items.q: What defines a reactive non-stress test (NST) in a fetus at 36 weeks gestation?
o: At least 2 fetal heart rate accelerations of >= 15 bpm above baseline lasting >= 15 seconds within a 20-minute window
Absence of any fetal movements over 40 minutes
A continuous flat baseline with variability < 3 bpm
At least 5 variable decelerations within 10 minutes
items.exp: In a fetus at or beyond 32 weeks gestation, a reactive (reassuring) non-stress test requires at least 2 accelerations of the fetal heart rate of at least 15 beats per minute above baseline, each lasting at least 15 seconds (the 15x15 rule), within a 20-minute monitoring window. (Prior to 32 weeks, 10x10 is acceptable).
r: Correct. A reactive NST requires at least 2 accelerations of >= 15 bpm lasting >= 15 seconds within 20 minutes.
Incorrect. Absent movements indicates non-reactive trace.
Incorrect. Flat baseline reflects absent variability, abnormal.
Incorrect. Variable decelerations indicate cord compression, not reactivity.
items.kp: A reactive NST requires at least two 15 bpm accelerations lasting >= 15 seconds within 20 minutes (15x15 rule).

items.q: What is the most common benign non-pathological cause of transiently reduced fetal heart rate variability (< 5 bpm) lasting for 20 to 40 minutes on an otherwise normal CTG trace?
o: Normal fetal non-REM quiet sleep state
items.exp: The most frequent benign cause of reduced FHR variability is the physiological fetal quiet (non-REM) sleep cycle. Normal fetal sleep cycles typically last 20 to 40 minutes (rarely up to 50-60 minutes). In the absence of decelerations, extending the trace or applying vibroacoustic stimulation wakes the fetus and restores normal variability.
r: Correct. Physiological quiet sleep cycles last 20-40 minutes and cause transient reduced variability without hypoxia.
Incorrect. Metabolic acidemia causes persistent absent variability accompanied by late decelerations.
Incorrect. Dehydration causes maternal tachycardia, not isolated transient loss of variability.
Incorrect. Abruption causes painful bleeding and hypertonic contractions.
items.kp: Normal fetal quiet sleep cycles last 20 to 40 minutes and are the most common cause of transient reduced variability.

items.q: Which medication is specifically administered to a mother experiencing uterine hyperstimulation (tachysystole with > 5 contractions in 10 minutes) causing prolonged fetal bradycardia?
items.exp: Uterine tachysystole (> 5 contractions in 10 minutes) compromises placental blood flow during relaxation, leading to acute fetal hypoxia and bradycardia. After discontinuing any running oxytocin infusion, acute tocolysis with a rapid-acting beta-2 agonist like subcutaneous Terbutaline (0.25 mg) relaxes the myometrium within minutes, restoring placental perfusion.
r: Correct. Terbutaline (0.25 mg SC) rapidly abolishes uterine tachysystole, restoring uteroplacental blood flow.
Incorrect. Oxytocin would further increase contractions, worsening fatal hypoxia.
Incorrect. Ergotamine causes tetanic uterine spasm and is strictly contraindicated before fetal delivery.
Incorrect. Magnesium is slower in onset than terbutaline for acute tocolytic rescue.
items.kp: Subcutaneous Terbutaline (0.25 mg) is the acute tocolytic of choice to reverse uterine tachysystole and fetal bradycardia.

items.q: What is the clinical significance of 'shouldering' (transient acceleration preceding and following a variable deceleration) on cardiotocography?
o: It is a reassuring sign representing intact compensatory autonomic baroreceptor responses to cord compression
It indicates severe pre-terminal fetal cerebral edema
It confirms co-existing fetal cardiac rhabdomyoma
items.exp: Shouldering refers to brief accelerations immediately before and after a variable deceleration. It occurs when initial partial compression of the low-pressure umbilical vein reduces venous return, triggering a compensatory sympathetic heart rate spike before complete arterial occlusion causes vagal deceleration. Presence of shouldering indicates an intact, responsive autonomic nervous system.
r: Correct. Shouldering is a reassuring autonomic response indicating an intact fetal neurological system.
Incorrect. It does not indicate cerebral edema.
Incorrect. It is not associated with rhabdomyomas (which cause dysrhythmias).
Incorrect. Loss of shouldering with blunted return indicates worsening hypoxia.
items.kp: Shouldering around variable decelerations is a reassuring sign of intact fetal autonomic compensation.
